$comment: Bilingual type is the part of this checkpoint most likely to be got wrong quietly.
Bengali is not Latin at a different size. Its glyphs hang from a headstroke (মাত্রা)
rather than sitting on a baseline, and vowel signs and conjuncts extend well above
and below the x-height. Set Bengali at a Latin line-height and the matras of one line
touch the descenders of the line above - legible in a sentence, unreadable in a dense
clinical table, which is where this system lives.
So every step carries a line height per script, and the build emits both. A layout
that switches language switches line height with it.
Both under the SIL Open Font License, chosen deliberately over a licensed pairing:
this is a commercial clinical system that will be deployed to devices the clinic
owns, and a font licence that has to be counted per-seat is a liability nobody will
remember to renew.
Bundled with the application, never loaded from a CDN and never left to the device.
A station tablet may be offline for a whole clinic session, and a font that fails to
load falls back to whatever Android has - which for Bengali is frequently a face
with poor conjunct coverage, so text silently degrades into broken ligatures.

latin.$why: Designed for screen UI at small sizes, with unambiguous 1/l/I and 0/O - which matters when the characters are a dose.

bengali.source: Noto Sans Bengali, SIL Open Font License 1.1
bengali.$why: The widest conjunct coverage available under a free licence, and the reference implementation for Bengali shaping. Validate on a real low-end Android device before Phase 1 ships, not only in a browser.

mono.source: JetBrains Mono, SIL Open Font License 1.1
mono.$why: For identifiers and codes - patient IDs, prescription QR payloads - where character-by-character comparison happens and proportional spacing hides a difference.

$comment: OPEN DECISION, surfaced at CP09 and defaulted here rather than decided silently.
Bengali has its own digits (০১২৩৪৫৬৭৮৯) and they are normal in Bengali prose. The
question is whether a clinical value rendered in a Bengali interface shows 7.8 or
৭.৮ - and it is not a typographic preference. A glucose reading transcribed onto a
paper chart, read back over a phone, or compared against a lab printout that uses
ASCII digits is a place where two numeral systems in circulation is a transcription
error waiting to happen.
Default below: ASCII digits for anything that is a measurement, a dose, a date or an
identifier, in both languages. Bengali digits are permitted only in running prose
where no value is being communicated. Needs Dr. Nahid's confirmation.
A 1.2 minor-third scale, rounded to whole pixels. Fractional font sizes render
inconsistently across Android WebView versions, and 'consistent' beats 'exactly on
the ratio'.
lineHeight is unitless (a multiplier of font size). Bengali runs 0.15-0.2 higher
than Latin at every step; the gap widens at small sizes, where matras and
descenders have proportionally less room.

weight.$comment: Four weights, not nine. Every additional weight is another font file on a tablet that may be loading over a slow connection, and semibold plus bold covers every emphasis this interface needs.

$comment: Named roles so a component says 'clinicalValue' rather than '2xl semibold mono'.
clinicalValue is its own role for a reason: it is tabular-figure, higher-contrast
and never below 16px, because it is the text whose misreading changes a decision.

clinicalValue.$why: Latin family and tabular figures regardless of interface language: digits must align in a column and must not change shape when the language toggles.
